suggestedQuestions: How can I separate sand from water?

slos.outcome: Describe a mixture and give everyday examples
Tell apart pure substances, uniform mixtures and non-uniform mixtures
Choose a suitable method to separate a simple mixture

suggestedQuestions: Is water an element or a compound?
How are metals different from non-metals?

slos.outcome: Describe an element and name common elements with their symbols
Describe a compound and tell compounds apart from mixtures
Sort elements into metals and non-metals using their properties

items.title: What is a mixture?
items.body: A mixture is made when two or more substances are put together without joining chemically. Each substance in a mixture keeps its own properties. In salt water, the salt is still salty and the water is still wet. Because the substances are not chemically joined, a mixture can be separated again by physical methods such as sieving, filtering or evaporating. The amounts in a mixture can also change: you can make tea with one spoon of sugar or with three, and it is still a mixture of tea and sugar. Mixtures are all around us. Air is a mixture of gases such as nitrogen and oxygen. Soil is a mixture of sand, clay, humus, water and air. Githeri is a mixture of maize and beans, and sea water at Mombasa is a mixture of water and salts.

items.title: Uniform and non-uniform mixtures
items.body: Some mixtures look the same all the way through. These are uniform mixtures. Salt water and sugar dissolved in tea are uniform: every sip tastes the same and you cannot see the separate parts. A uniform mixture of a solid dissolved in a liquid is called a solution. The substance that dissolves, such as salt, is the solute. The liquid it dissolves in, such as water, is the solvent. Other mixtures are not the same all the way through. These are non-uniform mixtures. Githeri is a non-uniform mixture, not a uniform one: you can see the maize and the beans. In muddy water, the soil slowly settles at the bottom. In soil you can see stones, sand and bits of dead plants. A quick test: if you can see the different parts, or they separate when left to stand, the mixture is non-uniform.

items.title: Pure substances and separating mixtures
items.body: A pure substance is made of only one kind of matter. Pure water, gold, oxygen and table salt on its own are pure substances. A mixture contains two or more substances, so it can be separated. We choose a method that uses a difference between the substances. Sieving separates pieces of different sizes. The holes in a sieve let small pieces through and hold back big ones. Stones are too big to pass through the holes, so they stay on the sieve, while the sand falls through. Filtering separates a solid that does not dissolve from a liquid: muddy water is poured through filter paper, the soil stays on the paper and clear water passes through. Evaporation gets a dissolved solid back from a solution: when salt water is heated, the water turns to vapour and the salt is left behind. A magnet separates iron from things that are not magnetic, such as iron filings from sand. Decanting means pouring off a liquid gently, leaving the settled solid at the bottom.

items.title: Worked example: getting clean salt from salty sand
items.body: Problem: Amina has a mixture of sand and salt. How can she get clean, dry salt? Step 1: Add water and stir. The salt dissolves but the sand does not. Step 2: Filter the mixture. The sand stays on the filter paper. The salt solution, called the filtrate, passes through. Step 3: Heat the filtrate in an evaporating dish until the water has evaporated. Clean salt is left in the dish. Why it works: salt dissolves in water but sand does not, so filtering separates them; then evaporation separates the salt from the water.

items.title: Misconception: a mixture is things that don't mix
items.body: Some learners think a mixture is made of things that do not mix, like oil and water. This is not right. The substances in a mixture are mixed together; they are just not joined chemically. Some mixtures mix completely: salt water looks like plain water, yet it is still a mixture because the salt can be got back by evaporation. Others, like githeri or sand and water, mix less evenly. Both are mixtures.

items.title: Misconception: dissolved sugar disappears
items.body: When sugar dissolves in tea, it seems to disappear. It does not. The sugar breaks into particles too small to see and spreads through the tea. You can tell it is still there because the tea tastes sweet. If you weigh the water and sugar before mixing and the sugar solution after, the mass is the same. If you evaporate the water, the sugar is left behind.

items.prompt: Which of these is a mixture?
hints: A mixture has two or more substances that are not chemically joined.
items.explanation: Salt water contains two substances, salt and water, and the salt can be got back by evaporation. Pure water, gold and oxygen are each one pure substance.

items.prompt: True or false: when salt dissolves in water, the salt is destroyed.
hints: Think about how salt water tastes.
items.explanation: False. The salt breaks into particles too small to see, but it is still there: the water tastes salty, and evaporating the water leaves the salt behind.

items.prompt: Which is the best way to separate iron filings from sand?
hints: Which of the two is attracted to a magnet?
items.explanation: Iron is magnetic and sand is not, so a magnet pulls out the iron filings and leaves the sand.

items.prompt: Which of these is a uniform mixture?
hints: A uniform mixture looks the same all the way through.
items.explanation: Sugar dissolved in tea is a solution: it looks and tastes the same throughout. In githeri, soil, and sand and water you can see the different parts.

items.prompt: Wanjiku dissolves 20 g of salt in 100 g of water. What is the mass of the salt water, in grams?
hints: Does dissolving add or remove any mass?
items.explanation: Dissolving does not destroy the salt, so no mass is lost: 20 g + 100 g = 120 g.

items.prompt: How can you get salt back from salt water?
hints: The salt has dissolved, so it will pass through filter paper.
items.explanation: Heating the salt water makes the water evaporate and leaves the salt behind. Filtering and sieving cannot catch dissolved salt, and salt is not magnetic.

items.title: What is an element?
items.body: An element is a pure substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances. Each element is made of only one kind of atom. Scientists know of 118 elements, and everything around us is made from them. Oxygen, carbon, iron, copper, aluminium and gold are elements. Each element has a chemical symbol of one or two letters. The first letter is always a capital and the second is small. Hydrogen is H, oxygen is O, carbon is C, nitrogen is N, aluminium is Al and chlorine is Cl. Some symbols come from old Latin names: iron is Fe (ferrum), copper is Cu (cuprum), sodium is Na (natrium) and gold is Au (aurum). All the elements are arranged in a chart called the periodic table.

items.title: What is a compound?
items.body: A compound is made when two or more elements join chemically. Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen. Its formula, H2O, shows that each water molecule has two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom, and this ratio is always the same. Carbon dioxide, the gas we breathe out, is a compound of carbon and oxygen. Table salt is a compound called sodium chloride. A compound has new properties, different from the elements it is made of. Sodium is a soft metal that reacts strongly with water, and chlorine is a poisonous green gas, yet together they make salt that we can eat. Hydrogen and oxygen are both gases, but water is a liquid. A compound cannot be separated by sieving, filtering or evaporating. It can only be broken into its elements by a chemical change, such as passing electricity through water.

items.title: Metals and non-metals
items.body: Elements can be sorted into metals and non-metals. Metals such as iron, copper, aluminium and gold are shiny. They conduct heat and electricity, which is why cooking sufurias are made of aluminium and electric wires are made of copper. Metals can be hammered into sheets without breaking, and they make a ringing sound when struck. Non-metals such as oxygen, nitrogen, carbon and sulphur have the opposite properties. Many are gases. Solid non-metals, such as sulphur, are dull, not shiny, and break easily when hit. Most non-metals do not conduct heat or electricity. One exception is graphite, a form of carbon used in pencils, which conducts electricity.

items.title: Worked example: iron and sulphur, mixture or compound?
items.body: Problem: How can we show the difference between a mixture of iron and sulphur and the compound they make? Step 1: Stir iron filings into yellow sulphur powder. You can still see grey and yellow bits. A magnet pulls the iron out, so this is a mixture. Step 2: Your teacher heats some of the mixture strongly. It glows and turns into a black solid called iron sulphide. Step 3: Hold a magnet over the black solid. It does not pull out any iron. Why it works: in the mixture, the iron and sulphur are not joined, so each keeps its own properties. When heated, they join chemically to make a compound with new properties, so the magnet can no longer separate them.

items.title: Misconception: a compound is a mixture of elements
items.body: Some learners think a compound is just elements mixed together. This is not right. In a mixture, the substances are not joined, each keeps its own properties, the amounts can change, and they can be separated by physical methods. In a compound, the elements are joined chemically, always in the same ratio, the compound has new properties, and it can only be separated by a chemical change. Salt water is a mixture of salt and water, but salt itself is a compound of sodium and chlorine.

items.title: Misconception: water and air are elements
items.body: Long ago, people thought water and air were elements. They are not. Water is a compound: passing electricity through water breaks it into two elements, hydrogen and oxygen. Air is a mixture of gases, mostly nitrogen and oxygen, with some carbon dioxide and water vapour. Its gases are not joined chemically, and the amounts change from place to place.

items.prompt: Which of these is an element?
hints: An element cannot be broken down into simpler substances.
items.explanation: Copper is an element: it is made of only one kind of atom and cannot be broken into simpler substances. Water and carbon dioxide are compounds, and salt water is a mixture.

items.prompt: What is the chemical symbol for iron?
hints: The symbol comes from iron's old Latin name, ferrum.
items.explanation: Iron's symbol is Fe, from its old Latin name ferrum.

items.prompt: True or false: water is an element.
hints: Can water be broken into simpler substances?
items.explanation: False. Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen. Passing electricity through water breaks it into these two elements.

items.prompt: Which property shows that copper is a metal?
hints: Think about why electric wires are made of copper.
items.explanation: Copper conducts electricity, which is a property of metals. That is why electric wires are made of copper.

items.prompt: Each water molecule (H2O) has 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom. How many hydrogen atoms are in 5 water molecules?
hints: Multiply the number of molecules by the hydrogen atoms in each one.
items.explanation: Each water molecule has 2 hydrogen atoms, so 5 molecules have 5 × 2 = 10 hydrogen atoms. The ratio in a compound is always the same.

items.prompt: Iron filings and sulphur are heated and turn into iron sulphide. Why can a magnet no longer pull out the iron?
choices: The iron is now chemically joined in a compound
hints: What happens to the iron and sulphur when they are heated together?
items.explanation: When heated, the iron and sulphur join chemically to make a compound with new properties, so the iron can no longer be pulled out by a magnet.
